Supply means the amount of something that is available to be used, bought, or given to people who need it.

Think of it this way: if you have a box of candles at home, that box is your supply of candles. If a pharmacy has 200 bottles of medicine on its shelves, that is the pharmacy's supply of medicine. The word always points to an available stock of something — something that exists and is ready to be used or handed out.

In day-to-day life, "supply" refers to a quantity or store of something that is kept or available for use. You will often hear it combined with another noun to describe how much of that thing is available — water supply, food supply, blood supply, energy supply, oxygen supply.

"The town's water supply has been contaminated" means the water available to the town is contaminated. "We have a month's supply of coffee" means enough coffee to last one month. "The hospital's supply of medicine is running low" means the hospital doesn't have much medicine left. In every case, the word is asking: how much of this thing do we have?

In economics, supply has a more specific and important meaning. It refers to the total quantity of a product or service that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale, at a given price, at a given time.

A few things are crucial here. Supply is not just about what physically exists in the world — it's about what sellers are actively willing to put on the market. When prices go up, sellers are usually willing to supply more, because they earn more profit. When prices go down, they are usually willing to supply less.

You have almost certainly heard the phrase supply and demand. This describes the pushing-and-pulling relationship between how much of something is available (supply) and how much people want it (demand). When supply is high and demand is low, prices tend to fall — because sellers must compete to attract buyers. When supply is low and demand is high, prices tend to rise — because buyers must compete to get the scarce product. For example, during a drought, the supply of wheat drops. Since there is less wheat available but people still need bread, prices go up.

When "supply" is used in the plural as supplies, the meaning shifts slightly. Supplies refers to the materials, provisions, or equipment that a person, group, or organization needs to function or carry out a task. Think of supplies as "the stuff you need."

"The soldiers ran out of supplies" means they ran out of food, ammunition, medicine — everything they needed to keep going. "I need to buy school supplies" means pens, notebooks, rulers, and similar things needed for school. "The rescue team brought medical supplies" means bandages, medicines, and tools for treating the injured.

The subtle difference between the two forms: supply (singular) usually refers to the available amount of one specific thing — "the supply of oil," "the supply of nurses." Supplies (plural) refers to a collection of different materials needed together for a purpose.

"In short supply" means something is scarce — there is not enough of it available. "During the pandemic, face masks were in short supply." The opposite, "in plentiful supply," means there is plenty available. "Fresh vegetables are in plentiful supply this season."

"Supply chain" refers to the full journey a product takes — from raw materials, through manufacturing, all the way to the final buyer, including every person and process involved along the way. When a supply chain is "disrupted," something has gone wrong somewhere in that journey, making it harder to get the product. This phrase became very common during global events like the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Power supply" refers to the source or system that delivers electrical power to a device or building. "Check if the power supply is connected properly."

No matter the context, supply always carries one central idea: availability. It is always the answer to the question, "How much of this thing is there, and can we get it?"

In your kitchen, it is how much food you have stocked. In a hospital, it is how much medicine or blood is on hand. In economics, it is how much of a good sellers are ready to put on the market. In a military campaign or an expedition, it is the provisions and equipment needed to keep people going.

Whenever you see the word and feel uncertain, simply ask yourself: What is available? How much of it is there? Who is providing it? The answers will almost always lead you directly to what "supply" means in that specific situation.
